What If You Lived Near a Star With Seven Earths?

Episode 66 of a daily journey through the universe. 🪐
TRAPPIST-1: a small, cool red star about 40 light-years away with seven Earth-sized planets, all closer to their star than Mercury is to the Sun, several in the zone where liquid water could exist. What the James Webb Space Telescope is finding.

segments.text: Imagine looking up and seeing other planets in your sky, some bigger than our Moon.
About forty light-years away is a small, cool red star, barely bigger than Jupiter. It's called TRAPPIST-1.
segments.headline: A tiny red star

segments.text: In twenty seventeen, astronomers announced it has seven planets, all about the size of Earth.
All seven are packed closer to their star than Mercury is to our Sun. A year there lasts from one and a half to nineteen days.
segments.headline: Packed together

segments.text: Standing on one, you could see the others in the sky, some looking bigger than our Moon.
segments.headline: Planets in the sky

segments.text: Because the star is so dim, several of these planets are at the right distance for liquid water. Maybe.
segments.headline: Maybe water

segments.text: The James Webb Space Telescope has been checking for atmospheres. The two closest planets seem to have little or no thick air.
segments.headline: Webb is checking

segments.text: The outer ones are harder to study, and the answers are still coming in. It's one of the best places to look for a second Earth.
segments.headline: Still looking

segments.text: Red dwarfs like this live for trillions of years. Long after our Sun dies, TRAPPIST-1 will still be shining.
Tomorrow, the closest planet to us outside our solar system. Next stop: Proxima b. Which part surprised you most? Tell me in the comments, and follow for tomorrow's stop.
